"I will do the job in a way that finds out the truth. That is the only promise I can make to you. It is the same promise I made to your sister. It is the same promise I owe your mother."

"""
ts when his legs have decided for him.

"Read it," he said.

"Daniel."

"Read it."

Lucia read the letter out loud. She read it carefully and without performance. She did not skip the parts about him. The parts about him were not cruel. The parts about him were, in a way that was almost worse, fond. She knows Daniel will be hurt. She knows Daniel has carried the idea of this house in him for a long time. She hopes Lucia will be patient with him. She says she gave him money to make it even because she did not know any other language for fairness, even though she knew the money was not the same as the house. She says she is sorry she did not tell him herself. She says she was a coward about it. She says, at the end, please forgive me, both of you, for not being braver.

When Lucia finished, no one spoke for a long time.

Then Daniel said, very quietly, "I found a piece of paper. In her desk. The day after she died."

Asha did not move.

"It was not the codicil," he said. "It was a note in her handwriting. It said where the codicil was. It said, behind the bobbins in the sewing machine. I read it. I put it in my pocket. I went upstairs and I burned it in the bathroom sink and I ran water until it was gone."

"Daniel," Lucia said.

"I did not look behind the bobbins," he said. "I did not want to know if it was there. I told myself if I did not look, it did not exist. I told myself the note was nothing. A scrap. A draft. I told myself she had not actually done it, she had only tho
